questions.prompt: What is the main difference in scope between a Salesforce Admin and an Application Architect?
options: An Admin configures a single org to match a process; an Application Architect decides what kind of application and platform capabilities should solve the problem and how it should be structured to survive change
An Admin can only work in sandboxes; an Application Architect can only work in production
There is no real difference between the two roles
An Application Architect writes all Apex code personally, while an Admin never touches automation
An Admin only works with standard objects; an Application Architect only works with custom objects
An Application Architect's job ends once requirements are gathered
questions.explain: The Admin executes configuration; the Application Architect makes the upstream design decisions the Admin and Developer then build inside.
questions.distractorExplain: Option D confuses the Application Architect role with a Developer's job. An architect's output is a design and its reasoning, not necessarily the Apex code itself -- an architect can (and often should) specify declarative solutions built by an Admin.

questions.prompt: A stakeholder asks for 'a button that emails the account owner when a case is marked Urgent.' Per this course's requirements-analysis lesson, what should an architect do before designing anything?
options: Build the button and the email automation immediately, since the request is already clear and literal

Ask follow-up questions to find the underlying need behind the request -- such as why urgent cases aren't already getting attention, and what volume and timing requirements exist -- rather than building the literal request unexamined
Reject the request because a button is never an appropriate solution
Escalate the request directly to a Technical Architect, since any automation request requires that credential
questions.explain: A stated request is often a symptom of an underlying need; the architect's job is to dig for that need through follow-up questions before designing, not to build the literal words unexamined.

questions.prompt: Match each term from this course's data-modeling vocabulary to its definition.
right: A conceptual description of real-world business things and their relationships, independent of any platform
The one-to-one, one-to-many, or many-to-many nature of a relationship between two things
The states a business thing moves through over time and what triggers each transition
A nameable business thing with a persistent identity, such as a Customer or a Claim
questions.explain: An entity is a nameable thing with identity, cardinality describes a relationship's one/many nature, lifecycle describes state transitions over time, and the domain model is the platform-independent conceptual description tying all three together.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: Salesforce requires the Application Architect credential to be built on four prerequisite certifications: Platform App Builder, Platform Developer I, Data Architect, and ________.
questions.explain: The four prerequisites are Platform App Builder, Platform Developer I, Data Architect, and Sharing and Visibility Architect -- Application Architect tests whether a candidate can combine all four into one coherent application design.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about the build/configure/buy spectrum from this course's lesson on choosing clouds and features.
options: Configuring a standard feature that already fits is generally cheapest to build and maintain, since Salesforce owns upgrading and supporting it
Building fully custom is generally the most expensive option to build and maintain over time, since the project's own team now owns every bit of behavior
Skipping straight to 'build fully custom' without first checking standard features is a common, named mistake in this course
Buying from AppExchange should never be considered under any circumstances
Licensing type has no bearing on whether a design will actually work for its intended users
questions.explain: Standard-feature configuration is cheapest since Salesforce maintains it; full custom build is costliest since the team owns everything; skipping the standard-feature check is explicitly named as a common mistake. AppExchange is a legitimate option worth weighing, not something to rule out, and licensing is explicitly called an architectural constraint, not irrelevant.

questions.prompt: A development team has three Apex triggers on the same object, each written by a different developer, with execution order nobody controls directly. Which pattern from this course's design-patterns lesson addresses this specific problem?
options: One trigger per object, with that trigger delegating to a handler class, putting the architect back in control of execution order
Adding a fourth trigger to coordinate the other three
Replacing all Apex with Custom Metadata Types
Disabling all triggers and relying only on validation rules
questions.explain: The one-trigger-per-object pattern, with logic delegated to a handler class, solves exactly this problem -- uncontrolled execution order from multiple independent triggers on the same object.

questions.prompt: Put these options from this course's build/configure/buy spectrum in order, from the cheapest/most standard option to the most custom.
items: Configure a standard feature that already exists
Adapt a standard feature declaratively (customize fields, layouts, Flow automation around it)
Buy a mature third-party AppExchange solution
Build fully custom (a new custom object and bespoke automation)
questions.explain: The spectrum runs from configuring an existing standard feature (cheapest), to declaratively adapting one, to buying a mature third-party solution when a good one exists, to building fully custom as the most expensive option to build and maintain.

questions.prompt: A capability is going to be maintained by a different team on a different release cadence than the application it would otherwise be bolted onto, and would be useful to a second, unrelated business process. Per this course's application-boundaries lesson, what does this combination of signals suggest?
options: It should definitely be built as a brand-new Salesforce org from scratch
It's a strong candidate for its own application boundary, and potentially its own reusable, bounded piece, rather than being bolted onto the existing application
It should always be ignored, since boundary signals are never decisive on their own
It must be built as a managed package with no exceptions
questions.explain: Different ownership/lifecycle and reusability beyond the current context are two of the three boundary signals this course names -- together they strongly suggest a separate application boundary, even though no single signal is an absolute rule by itself.

questions.prompt: How does this course define scalability?
options: A solution's ability to keep working correctly and acceptably fast as data volume and concurrent users grow, not just at launch with a small test data set
How visually polished a solution's Lightning pages look
The number of custom fields an object is permitted to have
How quickly a developer can write the very first version of a feature
Whether a solution uses Apex instead of Flow
The total number of users licensed in an org
questions.explain: Scalability is specifically about sustained correctness and acceptable performance as data volume and concurrency grow over time, not a one-time launch-day measurement or a cosmetic quality.
questions.distractorExplain: Option B describes visual polish, which is unrelated to scalability. A solution can look polished and still fail completely at scale, or look plain and scale perfectly -- the two qualities are independent.

questions.prompt: A custom object has a Flow that recalculates a parent rollup by querying and summing every sibling record on every single child update. This object currently has 8,000 records but is expected to reach 10 million within two years. What does this course say about this pattern?
options: It's invisible at low volume but becomes a real performance and governor-limit problem as the child object grows large -- exactly the kind of scalability assumption that should be revisited as real volume data comes in
It will scale perfectly at any volume with no changes needed
This pattern is required by Salesforce for all parent-child rollups
This is purely a concurrency scalability issue, not a data-volume issue
questions.explain: This naive rollup pattern is specifically named as a scalability trap that works fine at low volume and degrades as the child object grows -- a data-volume scalability concern that should be caught and revisited before it becomes unmanageable.

questions.prompt: Match each quality attribute from this course's Chapter 2 to its core definition.
right: The deferred cost of a shortcut taken now in exchange for faster delivery
How easily a new capability can be added without rebuilding what already exists
How easily and safely a solution can be understood, modified, and extended by someone other than its original builder
Whether a piece of a solution actually gets consumed in more than one place instead of being rebuilt
questions.explain: Maintainability is about safely changing existing behavior; reuse is about components actually being consumed more than once; technical debt is the deferred cost of a shortcut; extensibility is about adding new capability without a rebuild.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: a single Apex transaction can issue at most ________ SOQL queries synchronously.
questions.explain: The documented synchronous SOQL query limit per Apex transaction is 100 (200 asynchronously) -- a real, verified governor limit that exists because the platform is multi-tenant.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about technical debt as this course describes it.
options: Deliberate debt is a shortcut taken knowingly, with the limitation documented
Reckless debt is a shortcut discovered by accident by whoever hits it next, with no documentation of why it was taken
All technical debt is automatically a sign of incompetent work
Legacy automation left running after Salesforce retired Process Builder and Workflow Rules is a named source of technical debt
Making debt visible, rather than letting it live only in one person's memory, is the single most important discipline this course recommends for managing it
questions.explain: The course explicitly distinguishes deliberate debt (documented) from reckless debt (undocumented, discovered by accident), names legacy Process Builder/Workflow Rules automation as a specific source, and emphasizes visibility as the key discipline -- but it explicitly argues debt is not automatically a sign of incompetence, since taking it on deliberately can be the correct call.

questions.prompt: Two team members disagree about whether a new feature should be built in Flow or Apex, and re-argue the general merits of declarative versus programmatic tools from scratch every time this comes up. Per this course's architecture-principles lesson, what is the actual fix for this pattern?
options: Escalate every single instance to a Technical Architect for a ruling

Agree on a standing architecture principle (such as 'default declarative unless a specific factor justifies code') once, so future disagreements become the narrower question of whether a specific case meets the agreed bar
Always default to whichever option the most senior person in the room prefers
Avoid ever building in Flow again to prevent the disagreement entirely
questions.explain: The lesson's core argument is that a standing principle, agreed once, moves the conversation from a general philosophical re-argument each time to a narrower, faster question about whether the specific case meets the agreed bar.

questions.prompt: A Lightning record page loads in three seconds total but shows nothing to the user until everything is ready, while a different page takes four seconds to fully load but shows key fields within half a second. Per this course's performance lesson, which page is likely to feel faster to the user, and why?
options: The four-second page, because showing meaningful content quickly can make a page feel faster than its raw measured load time would suggest -- perceived performance can diverge from measured performance
The three-second page, because total load time is the only thing that determines how a page feels
Neither -- perceived performance is not a real architectural consideration
They will feel identical, since both pages use the same underlying Lightning framework
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly distinguishes perceived performance from measured performance using this exact example: showing meaningful content early can make a slower-measured page feel faster than a quicker-measured one that shows nothing until fully loaded.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: per this course, designing for 'the next plausible change' rather than for every conceivable future requirement is the discipline called ________.
questions.explain: Extensibility is specifically about designing for plausible near-term change signaled by actual requirements, not every conceivable speculative future -- which this course distinguishes from premature abstraction.

questions.prompt: In a domain model, a Claim Line Item has no independent meaning or existence apart from its parent Claim record. Per this course's data-model lesson, which relationship type fits this situation?
options: Lookup relationship, because lookups are always preferred for new custom objects
Master-detail relationship, because the child record's existence and default sharing should be tied to its parent when the child has no independent lifecycle
No relationship at all is needed between the two objects
A many-to-many junction object is required in every case like this
questions.explain: Master-detail is the right fit specifically when the domain model's lifecycle says the child has no independent existence without its parent -- exactly the Claim Line Item example this course uses.

questions.prompt: Match each packaging term to its correct description, per this course's packaging lesson.
right: An explicit, declared reliance of one package on components defined in another package
A distribution package with IP-protected metadata, built for shipping a product externally with a structured upgrade path
The deliberate, non-technical line an architect draws around what belongs to one coherent application
A source-driven package with inspectable, modifiable metadata, built for modular internal application development
questions.explain: Managed packages protect IP for external distribution; unlocked packages suit internal, source-driven development; a package dependency is a declared reliance between packages; an application boundary is the underlying design decision packaging enforces.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: per this course, a review that approves a design without genuinely engaging the quality-attribute checklist is called a ________ review.
questions.explain: A rubber-stamp review defeats the purpose of review just as thoroughly as an unproductive argument, since it approves a design without genuinely checking it against the quality-attribute checklist.

questions.prompt: Put these steps from this course's solution design process in the correct order.
items: Requirements intake: functional requirements, non-functional requirements, and constraints
Domain modeling: entities, relationships, cardinality, and lifecycle, independent of Salesforce
Data model mapping: translating the domain model into actual objects, fields, and relationships
Design review: the design is checked by someone other than its author before build starts
questions.explain: The solution design process runs requirements intake, then domain modeling, then data model mapping, through automation/UI design and a quality-attribute check, ending with design review before build starts -- getting the business reality and schema right before automation and review catches cheap-to-fix problems early.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about this course's Harborline Rentals case study.
options: Service Cloud's Case object was rejected because its support-oriented lifecycle and audience didn't match the internal maintenance workflow closely enough
Equipment was mapped to a custom object because the standard Asset object didn't carry the rental-specific fields Harborline tracks
The automation stayed entirely declarative because the complexity factors from this course's declarative-vs-programmatic lesson didn't clear the bar for Apex, given the project's constraints
The manager-visibility dashboard was silently dropped with no documentation at all
Maintenance Request used a master-detail relationship to Equipment because a Request has no independent meaning without its Equipment
questions.explain: The case study rejected Case for Equipment's lifecycle/audience mismatch, used a custom object for Equipment, kept automation declarative given real project constraints, and used master-detail for Request-to-Equipment based on lifecycle reasoning. The dashboard was explicitly descoped and documented as a deliberate trade-off, not silently dropped.

questions.prompt: Per this course's UI design lesson, when is building a custom Lightning Web Component justified over assembling standard components in Lightning App Builder?
options: Only when a developer happens to be available with free time

When the UI needs something standard components and App Builder's composition genuinely can't provide, such as a highly specific interactive visualization or a component meant for wide, repeated reuse
Whenever the page needs to display any field at all
Custom LWCs should always be preferred over standard components in every situation
questions.explain: The lesson specifically reserves custom LWC development for needs standard composition can't meet -- highly specific interactions, custom visualizations, or genuinely reusable building blocks -- not as a default first choice.

questions.prompt: Per this course's documentation lesson, why does a decision record protect a design from being accidentally undone later?
options: Because it legally prevents anyone from ever changing the design again

Because without a record of the reasoning, a future developer has no way to tell a deliberate, correctly-reasoned trade-off from something that just happened to get built that way -- and might 'improve' the design by reversing a decision that was actually correct
Because Salesforce automatically locks any documented decision from being changed
Decision records have no actual protective effect on a design
questions.explain: The lesson argues a documented decision lets a future maintainer distinguish deliberate trade-offs from accidents, preventing well-intentioned changes from accidentally reversing a choice that was correct for reasons that may still apply.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: this course's lightweight decision-record format, adapted from the general software-engineering practice of Architecture Decision Records, covers four parts: Context, Decision, Alternatives considered, and ________.
questions.explain: The four parts are Context (what prompted the decision), Decision (what was decided), Alternatives considered (what else was on the table and why it wasn't chosen), and Consequences (what the decision commits the team to, including any debt it creates).

questions.prompt: Why does this course argue a designer cannot fully substitute self-review for an independent design review?
options: Because designers are never trustworthy enough to review anything

Because the person who built a design has already made its assumptions feel reasonable to themselves, so a gap they've stopped noticing is often immediately visible to a reviewer seeing the design fresh -- a structural fact about familiarity, not a statement about skill
Because Salesforce's terms of service forbid self-review
Because only Technical Architects are permitted to review designs
questions.explain: The lesson frames this as a structural effect of familiarity with one's own reasoning, not a trust or skill issue -- an independent reviewer hasn't internalized the design's baked-in assumptions.

questions.prompt: Why does this course avoid stating a specific current question count, time limit, or passing score for the Application Architect exam as fixed fact?
options: Because the exam has no format at all

Because these exam mechanics change between exam versions, and stating an outdated or unverified figure as current fact would be worse than not stating one, so students are directed to Salesforce's own official, current exam guide instead
Because Salesforce has discontinued the Application Architect credential entirely
Because exam format numbers are classified information
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly withholds specific exam-format numbers because third-party sources checked gave conflicting, dated figures -- directing students to Salesforce's own current official exam guide is the reliable path.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about this course's consolidated list of common application architecture mistakes.
options: Designing straight from a stakeholder's stated request, without digging for the underlying need, is named as a recurring mistake
Skipping design review, or treating it as a rubber stamp, is named as a recurring mistake
The course frames these mistakes primarily as knowledge gaps rather than process failures
Building generic, reusable structures before a second real use case justifies them (premature abstraction) is named as a recurring mistake
Making a significant decision and never documenting why is named as a recurring mistake
questions.explain: All of these except the knowledge-gap framing are explicitly named in the consolidated list. The course explicitly argues the opposite of that framing: these mistakes are process failures under pressure, not failures to know a fact.

questions.prompt: In this course's worked exam-style scenario about a logistics company tracking which driver delivered which package, why was a lookup relationship correct instead of master-detail?
options: Because lookup relationships are always technically faster than master-detail relationships
Because a Package has its own independent meaning and lifecycle regardless of which driver delivered it -- a package record shouldn't be deleted if a driver's record is ever removed
Because master-detail relationships cannot be created on custom objects
Because the scenario explicitly forbade using any relationship field at all
questions.explain: Applying the lifecycle reasoning from this course's data-model lesson, Package's independent existence from Driver is the signal pointing to a lookup relationship rather than master-detail.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: per this course's exam-scenario lesson, the most common trap in scenario-based architecture questions is choosing the most sophisticated-sounding answer instead of the one that actually fits the scenario's stated ________.
questions.explain: The lesson identifies the core trap as being pulled toward an impressive-sounding distractor instead of weighing the scenario's actual stated constraints -- volume, timeline, licensing, existing systems.

questions.prompt: How does this course's final lesson tie its consolidated mistake list back to Lesson 1's opening framing of the Application Architect role?
options: It argues Lesson 1's framing should be discarded in favor of a purely technical definition of the role

It connects every mistake on the list back to Lesson 1's distinction between a solution that 'works' and one that is 'well-architected' -- each mistake is a way a solution can pass the first bar while failing the second
It claims mistakes only matter for Technical Architects, not Application Architects
It states that exam preparation has no connection to the rest of the course
questions.explain: The closing lesson explicitly ties its mistake list back to the 'works' vs. 'well-architected' distinction from Lesson 1, framing every mistake as a way a solution can function short-term while still failing the higher architectural bar.
